questions.problem: Given that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are the solutions to the equation $\operatorname{csc}⁡x=-\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}$ for ${0}^{∘}\le x<{360}^{∘},$ what is the numerical value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that $\operatorname{csc}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x},$ therefore the given equation is equivalent to

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡x=-\frac{3}{2\sqrt{3}}=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.
$$

First, we find the principal value of $x.$ 

$$
x=\text{arcsin}(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})=-{60}^{∘}.
$$

This value is outside the required domain. To get a value inside the range, we add ${360}^{∘}.$

$$
{x}_{1}=x+{360}^{∘}=-{60}^{∘}+{360}^{∘}={300}^{∘}.
$$

So, our first solution is ${x}_{1}={300}^{∘}.$

Our first solution lies in the fourth quadrant and has a reference angle of ${\theta }_{R}={60}^{∘}.$ Since $\operatorname{sin}⁡x<0,$ the second solution must lie in the third quadrant, and it also has a reference angle ${\theta }_{R}={60}^{∘}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13978818/assets/5fe064cdc2d97e3db894801f6f31a4679881efcf83564e24a1ea2559c15d2085.png)

Since the second solution ${x}_{2}$ lies in the $3$rd quadrant, we can find it using the reference angle as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={180}^{∘}+{\theta }_{R} \\  & ={180}^{∘}+{60}^{∘} \\  & ={240}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solutions are $x={300}^{∘},{240}^{∘}.$

Finally,

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=300\cdot 240=72\,000.
$$

questions.problem: Given that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are the solutions to the equation $\operatorname{csc}⁡x+3=-1-\operatorname{csc}⁡x$ for ${0}^{∘}\le x<{360}^{∘},$ what is the numerical value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation, isolating $\operatorname{csc}⁡x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{csc}⁡x+3 & =-1-\operatorname{csc}⁡x \\ 2\operatorname{csc}⁡x & =-4 \\ \operatorname{csc}⁡x & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that $\operatorname{csc}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x},$ therefore the given equation is equivalent to

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡x=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Now, we find the principal value: 

$$
x=\text{arcsin}(-\frac{1}{2})=-{30}^{∘}
$$

This value is outside the required domain. To get a value inside the range, we add ${360}^{∘}.$ 

$$
{x}_{1}=x+{360}^{∘}=-{30}^{∘}+{360}^{∘}={330}^{∘}.
$$

So,  our first solution is ${x}_{1}={330}^{∘}.$

Our first solution lies in the fourth quadrant and has a reference angle of ${\theta }_{R}={30}^{∘}.$ Since $\operatorname{sin}⁡x<0,$ the second solution must lie in the third quadrant, and it also has a reference angle ${\theta }_{R}={30}^{∘}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13978818/assets/b3c523e882baf0b3a105e10131091e40de686b4c1483f46e7bdc235e30743a6d.png)

Since the second solution ${x}_{2}$ lies in the $3$rd quadrant, we can find it using the reference angle as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={180}^{∘}+{\theta }_{R} \\  & ={180}^{∘}+{30}^{∘} \\  & ={210}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solutions are $x={210}^{∘},{330}^{∘}.$

Finally,

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=210\cdot 330=69\,300.
$$

questions.problem: The solution to the equation $4\operatorname{csc}⁡x=3\operatorname{csc}⁡x-1$ for ${0}^{∘}\le x<{360}^{∘}$ is $x=${{field-1}}${}^{∘}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation, isolating $\operatorname{csc}⁡x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4\operatorname{csc}⁡x & =3\operatorname{csc}⁡x-1 \\ \operatorname{csc}⁡x & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that $\operatorname{csc}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}.$ Therefore, the given equation is equivalent to

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡x=-1.
$$

Now, we find the principal value of $x:$

$$
x=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(-1)=-{90}^{∘}
$$

Note that $x=-{90}^{∘}$ is not in the given domain. To get a value inside the range, we add ${360}^{∘}:$

$$
{x}_{1}=-{90}^{∘}+{360}^{∘}={270}^{∘}
$$

As this is a quadrantal angle, to find the remaining solutions, we use our knowledge of the sine function. We know that the sine function has its minimum values at

$$
x={270}^{∘}+n\cdot {360}^{∘}.
$$

Since the domain $0\le x<{360}^{∘}$ is one period, and we have already found one minimum value in this period, we conclude that 
$x={270}^{∘}$
is the only solution.

questions.problem: Given that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are the solutions to the equation $\operatorname{csc}⁡x=\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}$ for $0\le x<2\pi ,$ what is the value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that $\operatorname{csc}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x},$ therefore the given equation is equivalent to

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡x=\frac{3}{2\sqrt{3}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.
$$

First, we find the principal value:

$$
x=\text{arcsin}(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})=\frac{\pi }{3}.
$$

Since $\frac{\pi }{3}$ lies inside the required domain, our first solution is ${x}_{1}=\frac{\pi }{3}.$

Our first solution lies in the  first quadrant and has a reference angle of ${\theta }_{R}=\frac{\pi }{3}.$ Since $\operatorname{sin}⁡x>0,$ the second solution must lie in the second quadrant, and it also has a reference angle ${\theta }_{R}=\frac{\pi }{3}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13978818/assets/4cbf970747a9eddbcffe6fd3ba46d13c43e5f17ca56e52747c797229dbc74d48.png)

Since the second solution ${x}_{2}$ lies in the $2$nd quadrant, we can find it using the reference angle as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =\pi -{\theta }_{R} \\  & =\pi -\frac{\pi }{3} \\  & =\frac{2\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solutions are $x=\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{2\pi }{3}.$

Finally,

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=\frac{\pi }{3}\cdot \frac{2\pi }{3}=\frac{2{\pi }^{2}}{9}.
$$

questions.problem: Solve the equation $\operatorname{csc}⁡x=-1$ for $0\le x<2\pi .$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that $\operatorname{csc}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x},$ therefore the given equation is equivalent to

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡x=-1.
$$

Now, we have to find the principal value:

$$
x=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(-1)=-\frac{\pi }{2}
$$

Note that $x=-\frac{\pi }{2}$ is not in the range $0\le x<2\pi .$ To get the first solution that's within the required range, we need to find an angle that's coterminal with $-\frac{\pi }{2}.$ To do this, we simply add $2\pi :$

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{\pi }{2}+2\pi =\frac{3\pi }{2}
$$

As this is a quadrantal angle, to find the remaining solutions we use our knowledge of the sine function. We know that the sine function has its minimum values at:

$$
x=\frac{3\pi }{2}+2n\pi 
$$

Since the domain $0\le x<2\pi $ is one period, and we have already found one minimum value in this period, we conclude that $x=\frac{3\pi }{2}$ is the only solution.

$$

Now, we find the principal value:

$$

$$

Since ${19.471}^{∘}$ lies inside the given domain, our first solution is ${x}_{1}={19.471}^{∘}.$

Our first solution lies in the first quadrant and has a reference angle of ${\theta }_{R}={19.471}^{∘}.$ Since $\operatorname{sin}⁡x>0,$ the second solution must lie in the second quadrant, and it also has a reference angle ${\theta }_{R}={19.471}^{∘}.$

$$

$$

questions.problem:
Expressed in **ascending order** in radians, the solutions to the equation $\operatorname{csc}⁡x=-\sqrt{2}$ for $-2\pi \le x<0,$ are

$x=$
{{field-1}}$,\,x=$
{{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that $\operatorname{csc}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}.$ Therefore, the given equation is equivalent to

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡x=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.
$$

First, we have to find the principal value:

$$
x=\text{arcsin}(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})=-\frac{\pi }{4}
$$

Since $-\frac{\pi }{4}$ lies inside the given domain, our first solution is ${x}_{1}=-\frac{\pi }{4}.$

Our first solution lies in the fourth quadrant and has a reference angle of ${\theta }_{R}=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ Since $\operatorname{sin}⁡x<0,$ the second solution must lie in the third quadrant, and it also has a reference angle ${\theta }_{R}=\frac{\pi }{4}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13978818/assets/012f0986293e2a4318dc68633a4ac0e91732d74300496427aaaa6635b417efe4.png)

Since the second solution lies in the $3$rd quadrant, we can find it using the reference angle as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\pi +{\theta }_{R} \\  & =\pi +\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $x=\frac{5\pi }{4}$ is not in the required domain $-2\pi \le x\le 0.$ To get a solution that is inside the required domain, we subtract $2\pi :$

$$
{x}_{2}=\frac{5\pi }{4}-2\pi =-\frac{3\pi }{4}
$$

So, in ascending order,  the solutions are 

$$
x=-\frac{3\pi }{4},\,x=-\frac{\pi }{4}.
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following equations has no solutions for $0\le x<2\pi ?$

- $\operatorname{csc}⁡x=10$
- $\operatorname{csc}⁡x=\frac{1}{2}$
- $\operatorname{csc}⁡x=-1$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the range of $\operatorname{csc}⁡x$ for $0\le x<2\pi $ is given by

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡x\in (-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty ).
$$

So, the equation $\operatorname{csc}⁡x=k$ has no solutions for $k\in (-1,1).$ 

Therefore, of the given equations, only equation II has no solutions.

canonical_examples.problem: Solve the equation $2\csc x+4=0$ for $0 < x <   2\pi.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation, isolating $\csc {x} \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{csc}⁡x+4 & =0 \\ 2\operatorname{csc}⁡x & =-4 \\ \operatorname{csc}⁡x & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that $\csc{x} = \dfrac{1}{\sin{x}}.$ Therefore the given equation is equivalent to

$$
\sin{x} = \dfrac{1}{(-2)} = -\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Now, we find the principal value:

$$
x = \arcsin\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = -\dfrac{\pi}{6}
$$

This value is outside the required domain $0 < x <   2\pi.$ To get a value inside the required domain, we add $2\pi\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
x_1 = x + 2\pi = -\dfrac \pi 6 + 2\pi = \dfrac{11\pi}6
$$

So,  our first solution is $x_1 = \dfrac{11\pi}6.$

Our first solution lies in the  fourth quadrant and has a reference angle of $\theta_R = \dfrac{\pi}{6}.$ Since $\sin{x}<    0,$ the second solution must lie in the third quadrant, and it also has a reference angle $\theta_R = \dfrac{\pi}{6}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13978818/assets/85b7b73fa793153cfedb2ffdb6825edd0845f93dbb472404862a78476a56fc35.png)

Since the second solution $x_2$ lies in the $3$rd quadrant, we can find it using the reference angle as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =\pi +{\theta }_{R} \\  & =\pi +\frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =\frac{7\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solutions are $x=\dfrac{7\pi}{6}, \dfrac{11\pi}{6}.$

canonical_examples.problem: Find, in radians to $1$ decimal place, all of the solutions to the equation $\dfrac{\csc x}{5} -1 = 0$ for $0 \leq x <              2\pi.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation, isolating $\csc {x} \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{csc}⁡x}{5}-1 & =0 \\ \frac{\operatorname{csc}⁡x}{5} & =1 \\ \operatorname{csc}⁡x & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that $\csc{x} = \dfrac{1}{\sin{x}},$ therefore the given equation is equivalent to

$$
\sin{x} = \frac{1}{5}.
$$

Now, we find the principal value:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{1}{5})=0.201\,357…≈0.201\end{aligned}
$$

Since $0.201$ lies inside the given domain, our first solution is $x_1 = 0.201.$

Our first solution lies in the first quadrant and has a reference angle of $\theta_R = 0.201.$ Since $\sin{x} > 0,$ the second solution must lie in the second quadrant, and it also has a reference angle $\theta_R = 0.201.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13978818/assets/8bcd1ea412f9235a330f37ee9059a023d0ce9e03e2c38388875dc0c12afebc1e.png)

Since the second solution $x_2$ lies in the $2$nd quadrant, we can find it using the reference angle as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =\pi -{\theta }_{R} \\  & =\pi -0.201 \\  & ≈2.941\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solutions (rounded to one decimal place) are $x = 0.2, 2.9.$

canonical_examples.problem: Solve the equation $2\csc x + 4 = 0$ for $0 < x \leq   \dfrac{7\pi}{2}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation, isolating $\csc {x} \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{csc}⁡x+4 & =0 \\ 2\operatorname{csc}⁡x & =-4 \\ \operatorname{csc}⁡x & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that $\csc{x} = \dfrac{1}{\sin{x}}.$ Therefore, the given equation is equivalent to

$$
\sin{x} = \dfrac{1}{(-2)} = -\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Now, we find the principal value:

$$
x = \arcsin\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = -\dfrac{\pi}{6}
$$

This value is outside the required domain. To get a value inside the required domain, we add $2\pi.$

$$
x_1 = x+2\pi = -\dfrac{\pi}{6} + 2\pi = \dfrac{11\pi}6.
$$

So, our first solution is $x_1 = \dfrac{11\pi}{6}.$

Our first solution lies in the  fourth quadrant and has a reference angle of $\theta_R = \dfrac{\pi}{6}.$ Since $\sin{x}<0,$ the second solution must lie in the third quadrant, and it also has a reference angle $\theta_R =\dfrac{\pi}{6}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13978818/assets/85b7b73fa793153cfedb2ffdb6825edd0845f93dbb472404862a78476a56fc35.png)

Since the second solution $x_2$ lies in the $2$nd quadrant, we can find it using the reference angle as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =\pi +{\theta }_{R} \\  & =\pi +\frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =\frac{7\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

To get the remaining solutions in the given interval, we need to find angles that are coterminal with $x_1$ or $x_2.$ To do this, we add integer multiples of $2\pi$ until all solutions are found:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} & ={x}_{1}+2\pi =\frac{11\pi }{6}+2\pi =\frac{23\pi }{6} \\ {x}_{4} & ={x}_{2}+2\pi =\frac{7\pi }{6}+2\pi =\frac{19\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $\dfrac{23\pi}{6}$ is outside the required domain, so we ignore it.

Therefore, the solutions are $x=\dfrac{7\pi}{6},\dfrac{11\pi}{6}, \dfrac{19\pi}{6}.$
